claim: The Poisson generalized linear model (GLM) can be interpreted as a special case of the conductance-based encoding model (CBEM) in which excitation and inhibition are perfectly balanced.
source: Moreover, we offer a novel quasi-biophysical interpretation of the Poisson generalized linear model (GLM) as a special case of the CBEM in which excitation and inhibition are perfectly balanced.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is a central theoretical contribution of the manuscript.

claim: The CBEM can be fit to extracellular spike train data and used to predict excitatory and inhibitory synaptic currents.
source: Remarkably, we show that the CBEM can be fit to extracellular spike train data and then used to predict excitatory and inhibitory synaptic currents.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental validation with intracellular recordings as stated in the abstract.

claim: The CBEM predictions of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic currents were validated with intracellular recordings from macaque retinal ganglion cells.
source: We validate these predictions with intracellular recordings from macaque retinal ganglion cells.
evidence: The manuscript describes validation experiments using intracellular recordings from macaque RGCs.

claim: The Poisson GLM has provided a powerful tool for characterizing neural encoding in a variety of sensory, cognitive, and motor brain areas.
source: These models have found broad application to neural data, and the Poisson GLM in particular has provided a powerful tool for characterizing neural encoding in a variety of sensory, cognitive, and motor brain areas (Harris et al., 2003; Truccolo et al., 2005; Pillow et al., 2008; Gerwinn, 2010; Stevenson et al., 2012; Weber et al., 2012; Park et al., 2014; Hardcastle et al., 2015; Yates et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work demonstrating GLM applications across brain areas.

claim: In retina and other sensory areas, the tuning of excitatory and inhibitory inputs can differ substantially.
source: In retina and other sensory areas, the tuning of excitatory and inhibitory inputs can differ substantially (Roska et al., 2006; Trong and Rieke, 2008; Poo and Isaacson, 2009; Cafaro and Rieke, 2013), meaning that a single linear filter is not sufficient to describe stimulus integration in single neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies showing differential tuning of excitatory and inhibitory inputs.

claim: A single linear filter is not sufficient to describe stimulus integration in single neurons when excitatory and inhibitory inputs have different tuning.
source: In retina and other sensory areas, the tuning of excitatory and inhibitory inputs can differ substantially (Roska et al., 2006; Trong and Rieke, 2008; Poo and Isaacson, 2009; Cafaro and Rieke, 2013), meaning that a single linear filter is not sufficient to describe stimulus integration in single neurons.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observation that excitatory and inhibitory inputs have different tuning properties.

claim: The GLM can be interpreted as a conductance-based model in which a linear filter drives equal and opposite fluctuations in excitatory and inhibitory synaptic conductances.
source: Thus, to summarize, the GLM can be interpreted as a conductance-based model in which a linear filter drives equal and opposite fluctuations in excitatory and inhibitory synaptic conductances.
evidence: This is a theoretical result derived mathematically in the manuscript.

claim: An LN model can capture the relationship between stimuli and synaptic conductances measured intracellularly in ON parasol RGCs.
source: First, we establish that an LN model can capture the relationship between stimuli and synaptic conductances measured intracellularly (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2, where LN models were fit to intracellular conductance measurements.

claim: The LN model accurately captured the relationship between projected stimuli and observed conductances on test data, accounting for 79 ± 4% (mean ± SEM) and 63 ± 3% of the variance of mean excitatory and inhibitory conductances, respectively.
source: The model accurately captured the relationship between projected stimuli and observed conductances on test data, accounting for 79 ± 4% (mean ± SEM) and 63 ± 3% of the variance of mean excitatory and inhibitory conductances, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from fitting LN models to intracellular conductance data.

claim: The parametric soft-rectified linear function closely approximated a non-parametric estimate of the output nonlinearity.
source: We found that the parametric function we assumed (Equation 12) closely approximated a non-parametric estimate of the nonlinearity (Figure 3c black; see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing parametric and non-parametric estimates in Figure 3c.

claim: The CBEM predicted excitatory conductances with an average correlation of r = 0.73 ± 0.01 (mean ± SEM) when fit to spike trains only.
source: Using only a few minutes of spiking data, the conductances predicted by the extracellular model had an average correlation of r = 0.73 ± 0.01 (mean ± SEM) for the excitatory conductance and r = 0.69 ± 0.03 for the inhibitory conductance, compared to averages of r = 0.89 ± 0.02 (excitation) and r = 0.82 ± 0.01 (inhibition) for the LN model fit directly to conductances (Figure 5a–b).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from fitting the CBEM to spike train data and comparing predictions to measured conductances.

claim: The CBEM predicted inhibitory conductances with an average correlation of r = 0.69 ± 0.03 when fit to spike trains only.
source: Using only a few minutes of spiking data, the conductances predicted by the extracellular model had an average correlation of r = 0.73 ± 0.01 (mean ± SEM) for the excitatory conductance and r = 0.69 ± 0.03 for the inhibitory conductance, compared to averages of r = 0.89 ± 0.02 (excitation) and r = 0.82 ± 0.01 (inhibition) for the LN model fit directly to conductances (Figure 5a–b).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from fitting the CBEM to spike train data and comparing predictions to measured conductances.

claim: Measured conductances in ON parasol RGCs had nearly zero lag in their cross-correlation (0.0 ± 2.4 ms).
source: For example, measured conductances had nearly zero lag in their cross-correlation (0.0 ± 2.4 ms; see also Cafaro and Rieke, 2013), whereas the predicted excitatory conductance slightly preceded the inferred inhibition for all six cells (r = 12.6 ± 1.0 ms, Student's t-test p < 0.0001; Figure 5e–f).
evidence: This is a measurement from intracellular conductance recordings, also supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The CBEM predicted excitatory conductance slightly preceded the inferred inhibition for all six ON parasol cells (12.6 ± 1.0 ms).
source: For example, measured conductances had nearly zero lag in their cross-correlation (0.0 ± 2.4 ms; see also Cafaro and Rieke, 2013), whereas the predicted excitatory conductance slightly preceded the inferred inhibition for all six cells (r = 12.6 ± 1.0 ms, Student's t-test p < 0.0001; Figure 5e–f).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from analyzing CBEM predictions, with statistical significance testing.

claim: The CBEM predicted excitation preceded the average measured excitation by 5.6 ± 0.7 ms (p = 0.0005).
source: The predicted excitation preceded the average measured excitation by 5.6 ± 0.7 ms (p = 0.0005), while the predicted inhibition showed only a slight and statistically insignificant delay compared to the measured inhibition (r = 2.5 ± 1.3 ms, p = 0.11; Figure 5g–h).
evidence: This is a quantitative result comparing CBEM predictions to measured conductances with statistical testing.

claim: ON-midget cells have positively correlated excitation and inhibition with excitation preceding inhibition.
source: In contrast to the parasol cells, ON-midget cells have positively correlated excitation and inhibition with excitation preceding inhibition (Cafaro and Rieke, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior experimental work.

claim: The CBEM predicted the excitatory conductance in ON-midget cells with an average correlation of r = 0.85 ± 0.03.
source: The CBEM predicted the excitatory conductance with an average correlation of r = 0.85 ± 0.03 compared to the intracellular LN model with a correlation of r = 0.95 ± 0.003 (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from fitting the CBEM to ON-midget cell spike trains.

claim: The CBEM predicted inhibition in ON-midget cells with r = 0.33 ± 0.06.
source: The inhibitory conductance showed more nonlinear behavior than can be captured by a single LN unit: the CBEM predicted inhibition with r = 0.33 ± 0.06 and the LN fit to the conductance had a correlation coefficient of only r = 0.54 ± 0.07 (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from fitting the CBEM to ON-midget cell spike trains.

claim: The CBEM can discover positive correlations between excitation and inhibition despite being initialized using a GLM with oppositely tuned excitation and inhibition.
source: In summary, the CBEM can discover positive correlations between excitation and inhibition despite being initialized using a GLM with oppositely tuned excitation and inhibition (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the CBEM's ability to capture the positively correlated excitation and inhibition in ON-midget cells.

claim: The CBEM had higher spike rate prediction accuracy than the GLM for all nine RGCs tested (86% vs. 77% of PSTH variance on average).
source: The CBEM had higher prediction accuracy than the GLM for all nine cells, 86% of the variance of the PSTH on average vs. 77% for the GLM.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of model performance on spike rate prediction.

claim: The CBEM outperformed the GLM on log-likelihood for all nine cells, offering an improvement of 0.34 ± 0.11 bits/spike on average.
source: We then evaluated spike train prediction by comparing log-likelihood on a 5 min test dataset. The CBEM again outperformed the GLM on all cells, offering an improvement of 0.34 ± 0.11 bits/spike on average over the GLM.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of model performance on spike train prediction.

claim: GLM rate prediction errors were anti-correlated with the magnitude of the CBEM inhibitory conductance.
source: We found that GLM rate prediction errors (relative to the PSTH of the real neuron) were anti-correlated with the magnitude of the CBEM inhibitory conductance; the CBEM inhibitory conductance at times when the GLM spike rate exceeded the true spike rate was significantly higher than the CBEM inhibitory conductance at times when the GLM spike rate underestimated the true spike rate (t-test, p < 0.0001; Figure 7—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is an analysis of the relationship between GLM prediction errors and CBEM conductance predictions with statistical testing.

claim: The CBEM inhibitory conductance helped CBEM predictions by reducing the firing at times when the GLM over-predicted the firing rate.
source: This suggests that the CBEM inhibitory conductance helped CBEM predictions by reducing the firing at times when the GLM over-predicted the firing rate.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the analysis of GLM prediction errors and CBEM inhibitory conductance.

claim: Previous experiments have indicated that inhibition only weakly modulates parasol cell responses to full-field Gaussian noise stimuli.
source: Previous experiments have indicated that inhibition only weakly modulates parasol cell responses to full-field Gaussian noise stimuli (Cafaro and Rieke, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior experimental work.

claim: The GLM stimulus filter accounts only for the excitatory input received by the cell.
source: We compared the excitatory filters estimated by the CBEMexc with the GLM filters and found that the filters are nearly identical (Figure 8e). This indicates that the GLM stimulus filter accounts only for the excitatory input received by the cell.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing GLM and CBEMexc filters, which are nearly identical.

claim: The CBEMexc provided a superior prediction of the PSTH than the GLM (81% vs. 77% of the variance explained).
source: The CBEMexc still provided a superior prediction of the PSTH than the GLM (81% of the variance explained) and an increased cross-validated log-likelihood (mean improvement of 0.14 ± 0.10 bits/sp over the GLM; Figure 8).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of model performance.

claim: Retinal ganglion cells adapt to stimulus statistics such as contrast or variance.
source: Retinal ganglion cells adapt to stimulus statistics such as contrast or variance; increases in stimulus contrast lead to decreases in gain of the neural response, allowing the dynamic range of the response to adapt to the range of contrast values present in the stimulus (Chander and Chichilnisky, 2001; Fairhall et al., 2001; Baccus and Meister, 2002; Beaudoin et al., 2008; Mante et al., 2005; Garvert and Gollisch, 2013; Marava, 2013; Demb and Singer, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental work on RGC adaptation.

claim: Changes in the balance of excitatory and inhibitory input can give rise to multiplicative gain changes in neural responses.
source: Previous work has shown that changes in the balance of excitatory and inhibitory input can give rise to multiplicative gain changes in neural responses (Chance et al., 2002; Murphy and Miller, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical and experimental work.

claim: The CBEM maintained predictive performance across contrast levels more accurately than the GLM.
source: We found that the CBEM maintained predictive performance across contrast levels more accurately than the GLM (Figure 9c–d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing CBEM and GLM performance across different contrast levels.

claim: At 24% contrast, the GLM fit to all contrasts lost an average 0.36 ± 0.41 bits/sp compared to GLM fit specifically to the 24% contrast stimulus, while the CBEM lost only 0.16 ± 0.2 bits/sp.
source: At 24% contrast, the GLM fit to all contrasts lost an average 0.36 ± 0.41 bits/sp (normalized test log-likelihood) compared to GLM fit specifically to the 24% contrast stimulus, while the CBEM lost only 0.16 ± 0.2 bits/sp.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of model performance across contrast conditions.

claim: The CBEM predicted that excitation and inhibition were most anticorrelated at 22% contrast for the ON cells and 34% contrast for the OFF cells.
source: The CBEM predicted that, on average, excitation and inhibition were most anticorrelated at 22% contrast for the ON cells and 34% contrast for the OFF cells Figure 9—figure supplement 2c.
evidence: This is a prediction from the CBEM model fit to multi-contrast data.

claim: The CBEM predicted PSTHs more accurately than a Poisson GLM for spatio-temporal stimuli (83% vs. 79% average R2).
source: We found that the CBEM predicted PSTHs more accurately than a Poisson GLM (83% vs. 79% average R2; Figure 10e).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of model performance on spatio-temporal stimulus data.

claim: The CBEM predicted single-trial responses with higher accuracy than the standard Poisson GLM (average improvement of 0.07 ± 0.04 bits/sp).
source: The CBEM also predicted the single-trial responses with higher accuracy than the standard Poisson GLM (average improvement of 0.07 ± 0.04 bits/sp; Figure 10f).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of model performance on single-trial spike train prediction.

claim: Spatial correlations in the stimulus differentiate the CBEM's predictions from the GLM.
source: These results indicate that, although the GLM captures much of the RGC responses to full-field noise, capturing the inhibitory and excitatory synaptic inputs will aid in understanding processing of naturalistic stimuli which contain spatial structure.
evidence: This is inferred from simulations showing that spatially correlated stimuli produce different predictions between CBEM and GLM.

claim: The CBEM belongs to an extended family of neural encoding models that are not technically GLMs because they do not depend on a single linear projection of the stimulus.
source: The CBEM belongs to an extended family of neural encoding models that are not technically GLMs because they do not depend on a single linear projection of the stimulus.
evidence: This is a classification of the CBEM within the broader context of neural encoding models.

claim: The CBEM stands as the only model so far to have directly linked model components fit to spikes alone to experimentally measured conductances.
source: Although more flexible LNLN models may predict spike trains with higher accuracy, the CBEM stands as the only model so far to have directly linked model components fit to spikes alone to experimentally measured conductances.
evidence: This is a claim about the unique contribution of the CBEM compared to other models in the literature.

claim: The CBEM's linear-rectified conductance does not capture the non-monotonic portions of the stimulus-conductance nonlinearities observed in the data.
source: For instance, the CBEM's linear-rectified conductance does not capture the non-monotonic portions of the stimulus-conductance nonlinearities observed in the data (Figure 2c,e); this non-monotonicity likely arises from the fact that amacrine cells can receive inputs from both ON and OFF channels (Manookin et al., 2008; Cafaro and Rieke, 2013).
evidence: This is a limitation of the CBEM identified by comparing model predictions to data, with a citation explaining the biological source of the discrepancy.

claim: The reliability of RGC spike trains depends on the stochasticity of synaptic conductances.
source: However, the reliability of RGC spike trains depends on the stochasticity of synaptic conductances (Murphy and Rieke, 2006), and noise correlations between excitatory and inhibitory conductances may also affect encoding in RGCs (Cafaro and Rieke, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Bipolar cells that drive RGCs are known to be well-characterized by LN models.
source: An LN model for RGC conductances is plausible because the bipolar cells that drive RGCs are known to be well-characterized by LN models (Rieke, 2001; Demb et al., 2001; Beaudoin et al., 2008; Gollisch and Meister, 2010; Liu et al., 2017; Real et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work characterizing bipolar cells.

claim: The soft-rectifying nonlinearity closely matched the average conductance given the filtered stimulus value for excitatory conductances in ON parasol RGCs.
source: The soft-rectifying nonlinearity (dark blue) closely matched the average conductance given the filtered stimulus value (light blue points).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2C showing the fit of the soft-rectifying nonlinearity to excitatory conductance data.

claim: The soft-rectifying nonlinearity closely approximated the average inhibitory conductance as a function of the filtered stimulus value for ON parasol RGCs.
source: The soft-rectifying nonlinearity (dark red) closely approximated the average inhibitory conductance as a function of the filtered stimulus value (light red).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2E showing the fit of the soft-rectifying nonlinearity to inhibitory conductance data.

claim: The nonlinearity mapping membrane potential to spike rate was better described with a soft-rectification function than an exponential nonlinearity.
source: Note that although previous analyses of RGC responses using Poisson GLMs have shown that an exponential nonlinearity captures the mapping from stimuli to spike rates more accurately than a rectified-linear nonlinearity (Pillow et al., 2008), we found the opposite here: the nonlinearity was better described with a soft-rectification function.
evidence: This is a comparison of different nonlinearity choices based on fits to data, with a citation to prior work showing different results.

claim: The discrepancy in optimal nonlinearity choice may result from the fact that the GLM has a single nonlinearity, whereas the CBEM has a cascade of two nonlinearities.
source: This discrepancy may result from the fact that the GLM has a single nonlinearity, whereas the CBEM has a cascade of two nonlinearities: one mapping filter output to conductance, and a second mapping membrane potential to spike rate.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed difference in optimal nonlinearity choice.

claim: Midget cells receive OFF inhibitory input in addition to the larger ON inhibitory input.
source: However, midget cells receive OFF inhibitory input in addition to the larger ON inhibitory input (Cafaro and Rieke, 2013), and therefore a single LN unit could not completely capture inhibition in these cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior experimental work.

claim: The data showed a cross-correlation peak with excitation preceding inhibition by 10.1 ± 0.52 ms in ON-midget cells, and the CBEM showed a similar timing difference of 8.2 ± 0.8 ms (paired Student's t-test, p = 0.06).
source: The data showed a cross-correlation peak with excitation preceding inhibition by 10.1 ± 0.52 ms, and the CBEM showed a similar timing difference of 8.2 ± 0.8 ms (paired Student's t-test, p = 0.06; Figure 6f).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of timing relationships in measured and predicted conductances with statistical testing.

claim: The CBEM can capture key features of real neurons such as shunting inhibition and time-varying changes in gain and membrane time constant.
source: The resulting model, which we refer to as the conductance-based encoding model (CBEM), can capture key features of real neurons such as shunting inhibition and time-varying changes in gain and membrane time constant.
evidence: This is a claim about the capabilities of the CBEM model based on its biophysical structure.

claim: The CBEM outperforms the standard GLM at predicting retinal spike responses to novel stimuli.
source: We also show that the CBEM outperforms the standard GLM at predicting retinal spike responses to novel stimuli.
evidence: This is demonstrated through multiple comparisons of CBEM and GLM performance on test data.

claim: The CBEM differs from previous cascade modeling approaches by explicitly defining the model components in a biophysical framework and directly comparing model predictions to measured excitation and inhibition tuning in individual cells.
source: This work differs from previous cascade modeling approaches for separating excitatory and inhibitory inputs (e.g., Butts et al., 2011; Ozuysal et al., 2018; McFarland et al., 2013; Maheswaranathan et al., 2018) by explicitly defining the model components in a biophysical framework and directly comparing model predictions to measured excitation and inhibition tuning in individual cells.
evidence: This is a claim about how the CBEM differs from prior work, supported by citations.

claim: The CBEM has a well behaved point-process likelihood, making it tractable for fitting to extracellular data.
source: This conductance-based encoding model (CBEM) is no longer technically a generalized linear model because the membrane potential is a nonlinear function of the stimulus; however, the CBEM has a well behaved point-process likelihood, making it tractable for fitting to extracellular data.
evidence: This is a claim about the computational properties of the CBEM.

claim: The interaction between excitatory and inhibitory conductances allows the CBEM to change its gain and integration time constant as a function of stimulus statistics.
source: The interaction between excitatory and inhibitory conductances allows the CBEM to change its gain and integration time constant as a function of stimulus statistics (e.g. contrast), an effect that cannot be captured by a standard GLM.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the CBEM's capabilities, supported by the multi-contrast experiments.

claim: The CBEM can help reveal circuit-level computations that support perception under naturalistic conditions.
source: Thus, the CBEM can help reveal circuit-level computations that support perception under naturalistic conditions.
evidence: This is a claim about the potential applications of the CBEM.

claim: The CBEM models conductances and membrane potential as deterministic functions of the stimulus.
source: The CBEM models conductances and membrane potential as deterministic functions of the stimulus, which makes the likelihood tractable and allows for efficient fitting with standard conjugate-gradient methods (Real et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of a modeling assumption in the CBEM, with a citation to related work.

claim: All stochasticity in the CBEM is confined to the spike generation mechanism.
source: Another aspect of the CBEM that departs from biophysical realism is that all stochasticity is confined to the spike generation mechanism.
evidence: This is a description of a modeling assumption in the CBEM.
